Because he loved her, he glanced behind him.
She instantly fell back. Poor Orpheus
stretched out both his arms, trying to hold her
and be held.
- Ovid, Metamorphoses, translated by Ian Johnston

The sun scorches the earth, searing his skin as the air around shimmers ominously. He can hear the occasional groans from his people and Okhemans, buffeted by the unforgiving heat.

It seemed impossible that the black tide can withstand the swelter, but the scattering of refugees they chance upon proves otherwise, the only life for miles around in the hot wasteland. 

It’s still difficult for Mydei to accept, despite evidence to the contrary.

"There's plenty of life around," he can hear Perdikkas say, voice still clear despite time marching on, "Are the dry shrubs and venomous snakes not life? They could even be used for medicine, if you know your way."

"I think you're the only one who would be adventurous enough to create strange remedies from snakes," Mydei had countered, and Perdikkas only laughed.

He was strange, but Mydei never minded a man willing to try new things in saving lives; they had taken plenty of them, after all. Perdikkas had always given as much effort as the rest of them, diligent in creation and care, seeking to help defy death to further glory.

A child stumbles his way, and instinctively, Mydei reaches out to right the feeble body. Dark eyes peer from the small, grime-coated face; before he can say a word, the child is snatched from his grip— a harried-looking woman stares back almost accusingly.

"Kremnoan," the assumed mother spits, before issuing a few more curses.

Ladonian, his mind remembers, from the detailing of her clothing and unique style of jewelry known to these sky-worshippers, amid darkness and arrows from a time when he wasn't as haunted.

Perdikkas once told him that snakes could be helpful, their venom a balm. But Mydei didn't know his ways, and could not provide the cure needed for the poisoned arrow aimed at the part of his soul. A venomous snake can only stay venomous in his hands.

"He may be Kremnoan," a voice cuts in, quicksilver sharp, "but he is helping your people flee. I bid you to give him the respect you would give to any one of us."

Mydei sighs, but doesn't deny the tension leaving him slightly. "Deliverer," he offers, and Phainon only smiles back. It doesn't reach his eyes.

"Well?" He asks again to the woman. She bristles but gives a curt nod before rushing her child away, their forms mixing with the rest of her people as Phainon watches them and Mydei watches Phainon.

A bead of sweat rolls down Phainon's chin, dipping into the hollow of his throat. The urge to lean over— to taste— is dizzying, and Mydei glances away just as Phainon turns back, eyes brighter.

"I don't need your rescue every time someone has an issue with my heritage," Mydei says, feeling more than seeing Phainon inch closer. The heat radiating off the man is almost unbearable in their current environment; he wants to get closer, skin to skin, close enough to feel scorched by something more than Aquila's legend. He clenches his gauntlet hands instead, feeling the creaks ground him into reality.

This heat is driving him mad.

“Besides,” Mydei continues, “I do not blame her spite. The Kremnoan Detachment invaded their city once, after all.”

They continue their trek, dusty earth clinging valiantly to their clothes, before Phainon finally deigns to speak.

“Invasion or not,” he begins, and from the corner of Mydei’s eyes, can see the furrow set deep between Phainon’s clear sky eyes, “it doesn’t change the fact that you’re here now, helping them. There are bigger things to focus on, rather than a grudge of years long past.”

Mydei has to snort at that. “And what about your own grudges? You sincerely can tell me you’re not still holding onto the hatred of what happened to your home?”

“Her and her people are still alive. That’s what should matter now.” Phainon says, not refuting but still stubborn. He averts his gaze. “And perhaps… perhaps I did not want to take kindly to her unkindness to you. You and your people get plenty of that as it is.”

Obstinate. And naive, Phainon is.

Mydei still wants to keep this man’s heart alive.

“It’s difficult to forgive past conflicts,” Mydei says, tired suddenly in the heat, in this life. “The campaign has barely been a decade past. It may take more years and generations before things can be mended properly.”

“Mended how?”

“By accepting. Or forgetting. Whichever comes first.”

Phainon’s stare is steady. “And those options are the only ones?”

They’ve stopped now, the horizon a haze, the bustle of people far behind them leaving them alone at the edge of this world. Mydei has trampled over these grounds before, blood and strife following his heels like hounds of war. The concept of loss was not new, but Perdikkas’ death was an introduction to a series of acceptances Mydei was forced to honor.

He remembers the poisoned arrow, the rot encroaching on his brother-in-arm’s skin, the waning whispers as the night marched on.

He doesn’t remember where they buried Perdikkas in this dry, lonely land.

“It’s too hot to have these debates of trickery with you,” Mydei says brusquely. “If there’s nothing else out here, we’ll return to camp.”

“I thought Kremnoans could handle the heat.”

But Phainon gives a light smile, letting Mydei have his clumsy escape. And it is his hand, warm even behind the leather glove as they head back— tracing Mydei’s back like the kisses he frequently gave when they started their arrangement— that compels Mydei to speak by their campfire, flames flickering in each others’ eyes. 

"We used to sing and drink around fires like this, during the exile,” Mydei says, feeling more loose-lipped and limbed as his sweat cooled in the night. “Honey brew was the choice of drink for my companions and I.”

Phainon paused in nibbling his rations, looking far too invested in the admission. “You sing?”

Mydei’s stomach twists uncomfortably, surprised by Phainon’s focus on that part. “Used to.” When there had been those to sing to and for, to come back to and for.

“I bet I can sing better than you,” Phainon teases, as if sensing the grim territory of their conversation. “Made all the village girls swoon enough to follow me.”

At that, Mydei had to smile. “And the boys?”

“I’m charming, but I’m no Orpheus, unfortunately.” Phainon laughs. “But maybe that can change.”

The intent way Phainon looks at him then has Mydei’s blood rush to his ears, breath short.

“What, to find your own Eurydice?” Mydei scoffs, bringing his cup up to hide the tremble of his lips at Phainon’s ringing laughter again.

The tenderness in Phainon’s gaze is almost too much to bear. “Maybe so.”

And what can Mydei say to match that, beat for beat? 

But he will try, because that is their way. It is what Phainon deserves, his absolute from Mydei.

“Then tell me, Orpheus,” Mydei says, “Sing me something from your past. I will listen.”

Phainon is silent for a long moment, the flames caressing his handsome face in the shadows, his expression almost unreadable. Then, with a stuttering breath, he begins to sing, voice shifting from its naturally bright candor to something smokier and nostalgic. 

And Mydei listens, to the song about promises and hair cutting as a last honor; he watches, the nervous tic in Phainon’s fingers, the way his throat bobs and mouth shapes the music, the fond grief in those clear eyes.

He knows even before Phainon finishes that the song had a purpose elsewhere than just a fairy-like village, a song meant for a beloved gone.

“Who was it for?” Mydei asks, his own voice quiet in the aftermath. He knows that maybe he shouldn’t pry, but something in him felt honest to push, to give Phainon a chance to speak before he dances away in deflective poetry and teasing again.

“Well, for you now,” Phainon tries to laugh, but at Mydei’s look, quails before confessing, “My childhood friend, Cyrene.”

“She was important to you.” Mydei can understand. Perdikkas, Hephaestion, Leonnius, Ptolemy, Peucesta— they had been dearer to him than his own soul. He still can’t speak of them to the living, not yet. Seeing Phainon nod, he thinks on how this man is braver than anyone Mydei’s known, to suffer and still speak of love.

“Yes. It’s still hard to imagine this world without her. I… quite never had a friend like her, even now.” Phainon’s fingers rub at the wrist of his gloves, thoughtless and wandering. “She used to cut mine and her own hair. Wouldn’t trust me to cut hers, especially after I nearly made her bald in an attempt.” 

Mydei hums at the image in mind, amused. “A blademaster that can’t master shears? I can see it.”

“Hey, hair cutting is a specific art,” Phainon pouts, but he’s more at ease now. “She always held it against me, especially when I trained. ‘You’ll shave your enemies’ heads clean before they kill you yet, Phainon!’ The embarrassment did propel me to work harder, though. Not that it helped, near the end.” Because she’s still gone, are the unspoken words.

Mydei’s foot, sprawled out by its lonesome, is now accompanied by a certain Deliverer’s. The two rest against each other, side by side not touching, besides that sole point of contact. “I’m sure… that she’d never had a friend like you, either. But it was still worth it to her, even in the end. She wasn’t alone.”

Mydei’s never met Cyrene and there’s a certain arrogance in presuming— but in some way, he’s sure she would agree all the same. Mydei’s never met someone like Phainon before, after all.

Phainon’s foot taps against him, once, twice, before it hooks snug into the crook of his ankle. “I never had someone like you before, either.” The admission nearly shocks Mydei out of his skin, the uncanniness of their thoughts matching always a welcomed surprise. Phainon merely smiles, knowing. He leans close, close enough for his warmth to radiate and breath to glide over Mydei’s neck, his hair, the delicate whorl of his ear. “Maybe you found me first. The first time I saw you, I couldn’t help but trail your steps, to match you, strike for strike. If you sing, I’m sure I’m bound to follow, Mydeimos.”

Mydei can’t help the lone shudder before he shoves Phainon away, ignoring the other’s knowing chuckle. “Stop your jesting, Deliverer.”

“I’m not, I’m not. Everything I’ve said is true.”

“…Then your song being for me now, that’s true as well?”

Phainon merely smiles back. “I could never cut Cyrene’s hair in a way she liked, but in the end, all I could offer were some locks of mine to say goodbye, scattered to the winds. To honor as a promise to her, to keep living to remember her.” He moves closer, hand inching towards Mydei, and wordlessly, Mydei reaches back. “You and I, it… our hearts are kindred. I don’t know how to soothe the losses you’ve faced, but perhaps… this little song can accompany you.”

They lay in the night, watching the campfire begin its quiet death and making no move to rekindle the sparks. 

In a whisper, Mydei says, “Teach me.”

And Phainon does, no competition or lighthearted teasing in the light, only the whispers of an elegy in the shadows. Mydei hums along, feeling the way his own throat flexes, a long familiar and almost lost action as he finally begins to sing lowly, hearing Phainon fall silent to listen.

He’s kissed once he finishes, Phainon murmuring against his mouth, sweeter than pomegranates: “You win. I can’t compete this time, so I’ll follow instead.”

Mydei can only kiss back, sighing into Phainon’s mouth like he’s coming home and aching so fiercely for it.

It’s still dark when Mydei wakes and Phainon sleeps, curled towards Mydei’s body softly in the desert cold. He can’t help but to lean and stroke some hair away from that charmingly handsome face, only watching Phainon breathe. Just as the night begins to break, Mydei deigns to rise, mind stewing over the night’s matters.

The camp is beginning to rise, people wanting to beat the scorching sun’s heat as they bustle around; a fellow Kremnoan soldier sees him, face brightening as he tips his head in veneration.

“Prince Mydeimos,” the soldier greets, lighting up more at Mydei’s answering nod. “We’ve found no more refugees in this part, and the black tide is scarce. Both the Detachment and Okhemans have agreed to returning to the city. We leave in a few hours time, if there are no objections.”

A few hours time before they depart from Ladon. Mydei’s throat closes up at the thought, Perdikkas’ mellow laugh ringing in his ears. Then he’s reminded of Phainon’s song.

“Do you know anyone that cuts hair?” Mydei asks the soldier in response, and while the soldier peers back in confusion, dutifully leads him to an older, grizzled soldier with sharp eyes and deft hands.

“My prince?” She inquires, and his eyes hone to the shears clipped securely onto her belt. The Kremnoan Detachment’s local hairdresser in her spare time and fierce spearwoman most of the time tips her head, curious. “You’ve always had long hair, my prince. Beautiful, too, if you don’t mind my opinion. Is there a particular reason you’re in need of my services this day?”

“…Even I have to accept the heat of this place,” he finally answers, taking heart in the soldier’s surprised laugh.

“It’s a difficult thing, isn’t it? To accept things you’ve fought so hard against, hm,” she says, cheer in her voice as she gestures him to sit on a barrel. She twirls her shears, the metal glinting in the breaking dawn. “Don’t let the Okhemans know, they’ll never let you hear the end of it.”

Scarcely an hour later and a head lighter, Mydei wanders far to the edge again, gazing at the sun’s ascent in the clear horizon, the air beginning to take on its stifling haze. Strands of his once long hair, gold glinting bloody in his glove, trails behind him, scattering on the land.

They camp will return to Okhema soon, leaving behind Ladon to her lonesome. He’s forgotten where they’ve buried Perdikkas, time and grieving survival wearing away his memory to shame. 

But Phainon’s given him a memory and song as a guide; Mydei has to accept the gift as graciously as he’s able. One day he’ll let the memory of his comrades live on in someone else’s dreams; for now, he lets loose the strands of blood tinted gold, bidding a quiet farewell to Perdikkas, a testament to love enduring as long as Mydei is undying.

“Are you proposing something in particular, Deliverer?” Mydei asks, testy. Phainon merely stares back, a faint flush high on his cheeks. Then he laughs, the sound a mix of incredulity and something darker.

“If I proposed something… would you really accept? From me?”

The fight that breaks out after that is, in Mydei’s opinion, warranted. Even if some rooftops became collateral. 

***

Krateros sneezes as another wayward flower floats down on his head.

“This— this tomfoolery has gone on long enough,” he says, wrinkling his grizzled face as he surveys the populace bustling around with masses of flowers and celebratory goods. “Absolutely ridiculous in light of an upcoming war.”

Mydei demurely sips from his cup of pomegranate juice. “It’s a flower festival, Krateros.”

“Bah,” Krateros says. “Flowers.” He nonetheless accepts one from a giggling Kremnoan child before she skips away, grunting in affected discontent all the while. “A festival, they say, yet how can we fully enjoy it, hm?” Mydei doesn’t point out that Krateros nonetheless took said flower and placed it in the collar of his armor, participation in the festival be damned.

They sip their drinks in silence after that, cognizant of the council of elders’ presence around and the specific rotation of guards on their tail, watching the two men closely. The little girl from before comes back, grinning wide as she drags an Okheman boy along with her, the two clearly friends despite the prejudice directed towards them.

“Here!” She chirps and shoves the boy forward towards Mydei. “Meet our prince!”

Krateros growls like a guard dog, stepping forward but Mydei quells the motion with a sharp look. The Okheman boy, clearly nervous, cowers back, but Mydei gently leans, inviting the boy closer with a nod.

“Hello,” Mydei greets. “Are you enjoying the festival?”

The boy stammers, face bright red, and his friend just laughs, delighted by the reaction. “He says he’s never seen a prince before,” the girl says, gleeful. “Wouldn’t believe me when I said I could have him meet my own prince.”

“Hey!” The boy exclaims, and even Krateros’ stiff exterior cracks at the childish display. “You weren’t supposed to tell!”

“Then why are we even here,” the girl says, peeved. “Give your gift and then you can go back to hiding.”

“You—!” The boy fumes, but at Krateros’ beady eye, gulps, and shyly brings his gift out from behind his small back and offering it to Mydei: a crown made in white flowers. “This is— this is for you, Mister Prince!”

“Mister Prince—“ The girl guffaws, but Mydei breaks the oncoming scuffle by kneeling, offering his head for the boy to place the crown.

“I accept your gift,” Mydei says solemnly, but he smiles to soothe the boy’s nerves. It seems to do the opposite, with the way the boy gasps and turns redder. “Will you give the honor of crowning me?”

“Y-yes!” The boy stutters, and Mydei’s sure he also mutters, “This is the best day ever,” as he gently places his gift over Mydei’s grown again long locks. 

The group of children nearby starts to cheer at the display, and the boy jumps before fleeing, face flaming, as his friend follows with a cheerful laugh and expression of gratitude for Mydei’s time.

“Flowers,” Krateros says disdainfully, but even he seems to appraise Mydei’s new crown with some pride. “Not bad, for an Okheman child.”

“Accepting gifts so readily now, are we,” a familiar voice rings out, and Mydei turns, ignoring Krateros’ mutter of, “And here comes the distraction.”

Unfortunately, Krateros’ words are prove true with the way Mydei stops in place at Phainon’s appearance, eyes swiftly running over the man’s body with more than a little pleasure. Phainon grins back, looking especially sweet and flushed in the festive atmosphere. He’s dressed in a dark blue chiton that highlights the bright of his eyes; a white himation drapes over him, giving a regal feel rather than his usual battle clothes. A crown of flowers also lay over his white locks, pale blue with delicate leaves: myosotis, mouse-ears, or better known, forget-me-nots. Fitting.

“Hmph.” Mydei greets in turn, bringing his cup up to take another thirsty sip as Krateros gives him an unimpressed side eye. “As if you haven’t accepted gifts of your own, Deliverer.”

“Perhaps I was hoping to be the first to give the prince of Castrum Kremnos a celebratory gift,” Phainon laughs. “In the form of a drink, if you’re so willing.”

“I’m already drinking.” Mydei proffers his own cup, and Phainon merely comes closer.

“Maybe something a little stronger, then,” Phainon says, tone a little low. His eyes slid up and down Mydei’s body slowly, fixating around Mydei’s thighs, barely clad by the shorter length of his chiton. “Your clothes suit you, Mydeimos. It highlights your conspicuous body well.” 

Mydei fights to not cross his legs, unwilling to let Phainon know just how affected he feels, but the action is futile with the way Phainon smiles, a tinge predatory. 

“The prince does not ‘drink’,” Krateros butts in, frowning but unaware of the tension between his liege and Okhema’s hero. “It is part of his warrior’s oath. Therefore your gift is moot.” He made move to speak more but is interrupted by the gaggle of children from earlier once again, the Kremnoan girl— clearly the raucous leader of the lot— dictating Krateros show the Okhemans just what Castrum Kremnos is ‘made of’. He’s ushered off, grumbling all the while and giving Mydei a pointed look, but follows willingly.

The two watches him go, and knowing their turn to be monopolized by the youth is coming next considering Krateros’ inability to dance well, decides to bask in the revelry. Mydei watches Phainon, and Phainon watches back.

“Is it really a part of your warrior’s oath?” Phainon finally asks, raising an eyebrow, and Mydei sighs.

“No, I have no such oaths besides those of battle and honor,” Mydei says. “It’s just a habit.”

“Well, habits can be broken, even for a day,” Phainon says, and Mydei merely regards him with half-lidded eyes. Phainon leans close, the heat of his body familiar as Mydei’s own, if not more. “But in the meantime then, to emulate the children of this city’s future, accept this in light of Okhema’s great flower festival.” With a playful motion, he pulls a flower from his own wreathed crown, and offers it out with an expectant look.

“Flowers don’t last long,” Mydei observes, and a spike of regret crosses his heart at Phainon’s slightly crestfallen expression.

“Then that means you’ll accept it then, right?” Phainon tries, tone laced with bravado not felt. “Since it’s not forever.”

Nothing lasts forever, they both know that. The black tide, heavy respective fates, a flame-chase prophesied to end with much suffering and losses— they know the stakes and where they stand.

But Mydei wants one night, just one.

“I’m accepting this,” he says, taking the flower quick, amused by Phainon’s little surprised flinch. “But not because it’s not going to last forever. It’s a gift given by the great Deliverer— would be quite rude to refuse, I believe.” His actions bely his words, however, and Mydei’s ears burn at the riveted way Phainon watches as Mydei gently twists the flower onto his fourth finger. He struggles a little, one-handed, but Phainon’s own reaches out to help finish the knot. 

“Quite rude,” Phainon agrees, a little breathless; his hand is scorching on Mydei’s, twitching as if he wants to grab him and run far away together.

They’re interrupted by the children as predicted, and both are forced to separate to dance with their respective tinier partners.  Mydei knows Phainon is watching back just as intently, eyes a weighty thing. The steady heat between them builds, even as older citizens join the dance, the festival peaking with more flowers being rained and drinks flowing freely, and Mydei dances like it’s a fight, gives up being a prince of a dying kingdom for the night just to incite and provoke the man who gave him a precious gift. Many hands lay on him, in awe and desire to dance with a Chrysos Heir in pursuit of flames, but he makes sure the flower stays on, enduring valiantly despite the rapid waltzes, clinging to his finger as if everything will end if he loses it.

Finally, a familiar hand grasps his waist, and Mydei spins with a deep laugh, meeting Phainon’s barely restrained wild expression head on. His blood thrums, similar to when they trade blows and clash blades, and Mydei grins, all teeth, as he leans in to whisper, “Your gift is well received.”

Phainon shudders, eyes dark. “Then in return, I ask that you gift me something as well. Would that be fair?”

Mydei hums, draping an arm around Phainon’s neck, feeling bold even with keen eyes around. “Ask, then.”

“I want to eat,” Phainon whispers back. “Won’t you feed my hunger?”

Their dance comes to a gradual stop, slow as molasses, and Mydei regards Phainon with as much solemn decorum as he’s able. “Of course,” he says.

And that’s that.

They’re stumbling over cobbled roads, words lacking between them as they head to the outskirts of the city. The sounds of the people and festival fades away and quiets completely as they slip into Phainon’s residence. The homeowner himself is still silent, leaving Mydei’s side to methodically close windows against Kephale’s harsh brightness. 

Mydei’s inwardly berating himself for not swiping food off the tables— because what if he misconstrued Phainon’s statement,  he’d just left the man hungry if that’s the case and therefore unable to fulfill his request— before Phainon comes back and presses him, full-bodied, into the front door, stealing his breath better than Zagreus’ exploits ever could in legend.

“Deliverer,” Mydei says, after finally managing to pull away, a string of spit breaking between them.

“Mydeimos,” Phainon returns, hands gliding down to slip underneath Mydei’s chiton, encountering smooth, muscled skin. He squeezes and presses, seemingly drinking in Mydei’s sighs and little noises with great delight. “It should be illegal to wear this.”

“What, clothes?”

“You call this clothing?” Phainon says. “It’s barely covering anything!” Then his hands trail up higher and he chokes as he encounters no inner cloth, just more of Mydei’s warm flesh filling his hands. 

“I’ll have you know,” Mydei says, smug and paying for it when Phainon digs nails into his ass, “that this is appropriate wear for the occasion. From the royal seamstress, even, before the fall of Castrum Kremnos.”

“I highly doubt your royal seamstress planned for her prince to be wearing this and nothing else,” Phainon growls, incensed. “There were so many people at the festival, Mydei. They could’ve seen!”

Mydei has to kiss that frown away, annoyingly endeared. “Well, I was only intending for one person to see, and now he has.”

“Shameless,” Phainon shakes his head, but he’s holding back a smile.

“There is no word for ‘shame’ in the Kremnoan language,” Mydei tells him, “so perhaps that sentiment is true.”

“Is this the first time that Mydeimos, last prince of Castrum Kremnos, is agreeing with me with nary a fight?”

At that, Mydei hooks his leg around Phainon’s, coy with it as Phainon grips his thigh tighter. “Would you like to see what else I can come to agreement with, then?”

Phainon makes a truly broken noise into Mydei’s neck before peeling away and marching to the bedroom, flinging Mydei onto the bed. He’s peeling off his own clothes as Mydei laughs, before advancing onto the prince himself with a determined set to his mouth. His hands strike out, stopping Mydei from stripping as well, his grip tight.

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Are you revoking my undressing privileges?”

“Oh, you’ll be undressed completely later,” Phainon says, but he looks intensely focused as he examines Mydei’s form. “And besides, you’re naked enough to fulfill my request.” He lets go, and with deliberate movement, crawls to the head of the bed, and lays down, tapping the headboard with a pointed finger.

Phainon sighs as he reaches up to flip Mydei’s chiton up, baring him to dark eyes. He laughs as the headboard creaks warningly under Mydei’s grip, even as he licks his own lips and slides his hands over Mydei’s knees, thighs, and ass, pushing his rival up a little to position exactly right. Mydei breathes hard, restraint on a single thread, and then he sees the flower ring, more wilted than before but still hanging on. Mydei can’t bear to let it go, either.

Mydei doesn’t even question the lack of oil or further prep, already half out of his own mind with need, and he grabs Phainon’s cock, lifting himself up and sinking down on it as they both groan at the feeling. Phainon, in his hunger, did truly try his best to open Mydei as slick and wet as possible, but Mydei can’t deny the fact that he does like the burn, likes the work, likes the pain and pleasure Phainon gives him. He settles over hard hips, both of them harshly breathing, before Mydei rises up and starts riding him then, hitting his spots intermittently as Phainon watches him move, eyes blown wide and mouth open in panting awe.

I’ve wanted you for so long, Mydei.”

Mydei just bites at Phainon’s collarbone roughly in response, and the man moans at the gesture, length growing bigger in Mydei’s hole at the sudden pain. Phainon smooths a tender hand down Mydei’s sweaty back and flank, as he says, “That was… we are definitely revisiting that again.” Then he flips them over and proceeds to show Mydei what else he can deliver through the night.

Come morning, Mydei wakes to Phainon already watching him; the sun streaming in overhead obliterates any shadow across Phainon’s face, as if light is kissing that smooth skin. Mydei can’t deny the pang of petty jealousy at the thought that the sunlight touched Phainon before Mydei had a chance to. 

“You kept it,” Phainon says, soft, and Mydei follows his gaze to the flower ring on his own person. He chews his lip, the sight endearing. “It’s already dying.”

The flower died the moment it was picked.

But Mydei has accepted it regardless, it will not be given back.

He rises, just to kiss Phainon deep, hiding him from the light, wanting to steal a little of this man’s time even if it’s not forever.

“It was a gift from you,” Mydei says against his lips, giving another lingering kiss. “And I wanted it.”

The look in Phainon’s eyes is brighter than any everlasting sun in Okhema.

***

The conflicting disappointment, fear, and fierce determination in Krateros’ eyes is what gives Mydei the final confirmation that this is the correct path.

A signet ring lighter, Mydei wanders through Okhema, making his last goodbyes even as he takes in the signs of humanity around him. 

The other demigods’ and heirs’ resolves, the Trailblazers and their compassion, the children of both Castrum Kremnos and Okhema, united and cheering him on.

Only humans can guide the path to be trodden by humans indeed. His place is no longer with them, but, looking at the longing sorrow in Phainon’s eyes, Mydei can’t truly bring himself to regret this. 

One day, you shall die with a wound in your back.

It is fitting, that the one Mydei would ever accept his death from, should be granted knowledge of his weakness.

“But… if there’s a chance in the next life, you should come visit my library,” Mydei says, not a great believer in fate and weakness— but this, he wants to believe with everything, only to see Phainon again in any capacity. 

They make their farewells, but even despite that, there are still so many things he wants to say, to listen, to share, and to accept.

“One last question,” Mydei says, stopping in place and not turning around, but certain that Phainon is listening in kind. “Are you the one who told Chartonus about the signet ring?”

“Well,” Phainon says, already sounding further away, “…Who knows.”

Mydei can only smile at that, knowing that in his library, in a dictionary filled with Kremnoan lexicon, two rings are pressed in between its pages: one of bright white hair, and the other a flower that resembles a certain Deliverer’s eyes.

Mydei may have given away Phainon’s third gifted ring to his own people to find their paths, but he’s accepted the first two and that’s what counts.

A feeling rises up in his chest, and without meaning to, Mydei turns around just to see Phainon looking back. They both stare, taking in every last second and moment, before Mydei forces himself to turn and keep walking.

Phainon had been wrong, so long ago. 

Mydei isn’t Orpheus, no matter what Phainon insisted. The truth of the matter is, Phainon’s song and life gave something precious to Mydei. And like in legend, Phainon will look back because there is a world behind him, and Mydei will go as Eurydice did, fate tearing them apart despite the love still being there.

He’ll accept it anyway, as he did with every one of Phainon’s proposals and offerings.

Mydei walks back home alone, the light of Okhema behind him.

Now dying a second time, Eurydice
made no complaint at all about her husband
(what could she object to except the fact
that she was loved?).
— Ovid, Metamorphoses, translated by Ian Johnston
